nodes.label: localeProvider and languageEndonym
nodes.rationale: Holds a Locale? where null is exactly what MaterialApp takes to mean 'resolve against the system', so 'follow the device' needs no separate representation. A stored code the build no longer ships resolves back to the device rather than to a language with no translations. The picker is built from supportedLocales, so a new translation appears by existing; the one thing needed by hand is an endonym, because a language is listed under its own name and never translated — someone who has landed in a language they cannot read has to find their way out.

nodes.label: magnify_gesture.dart (one-finger drag magnifier)
nodes.rationale: Pinching needs a second hand a phone reader does not have. The artwork under the finger is carried towards it — one rule, not four cases, and there must never be an if (dy > 0) in that file. Drag length sets the magnification (2.5x over 400pt) and travel is absolute, because the ruler is a thumb and a thumb does not grow with the display. At an edge the border is held and the grip gives way, which is the normal case. That only holds because the reference point is clamped within travel/(maxScale-1) of the screen's middle; outside that band pulling down walked the view the wrong way by ~1.6%, and the anchor is the axis a test has to sweep exhaustively. The reference point comes from the pointer-down, never onPanStart, which reports where the pan was recognised ~18pt into the drag. drawnContent keeps the artwork rather than the letterbox against the edges. Page-turn swipes are gone while it is on, and vertical scrolling is excluded.

nodes.label: mockSecureStorage() in test_support.dart
nodes.rationale: On a test binding flutter_secure_storage has no platform behind it and the Linux implementation reaches for libsecret, which never answers — so a write HANGS the test rather than failing it, which reads as a stuck suite rather than a missing mock.

nodes.label: ProfilePreferencesStore (profile_preferences.dart)
nodes.rationale: Reading direction, magnifying and the interface language belong to a person; the image cache budget belongs to the device. Shaped like ProfileLockStore: one keychain value rather than a key per profile, read whole before runApp, a PreferencesVault injected, and the store instance handed to SessionScope so a mid-session choice survives a handover. Each notifier's build watches sessionProvider, so nothing had to be added for a handover and nothing can be forgotten on one.

nodes.label: The reader's cog and reader_settings_sheet.dart
nodes.rationale: A pill was right while direction was the only thing to say, but magnifying cannot be drawn as an icon and a second pill would eat the chapter title. The cog costs no extra tap, since the pill was a menu opener rather than a toggle. A sheet and not a PopupMenuButton, because a PopupMenuItem pops its route and a switch inside one would dismiss the menu as it was flipped; ReadingDirectionRows is shared with Settings so the wording cannot drift. Direction closes the sheet and overrides for this chapter only; the magnify switch stays open and writes the preference through.

nodes.label: ReadingDirection (verticalScroll is a direction, not a mode)
nodes.norm_label: readingdirection (verticalscroll is a direction, not a mode)
nodes.rationale: One setting decides everything and there is a single control for it. 'Webtoon' is Kavita's word and is gone from this app in code and on screen: what varies is the motion, not what is being read. verticalScroll rather than vertical because Kavita has two vertical readers and only the scrolling one is ours. The enum name is the persisted preference, so _legacyNames still reads the stored 'webtoon' — renaming a value without that is how a setting resets itself and says nothing. Never write LTR/RTL in UI copy.

nodes.label: SpreadLayout (landscape two-page spreads)
nodes.rationale: Which pages share a screen is not page ~/ 2: a scan that is itself a double page takes a screen of its own, or the spine would run down the middle of a drawing meant to be seen whole. A wide page shifts the parity of everything after it, so a step is a screen rather than a fixed number of pages and the counter's span comes from the page arrived at. The two pages of a pair are pushed together against the spine by Image.alignment, because centred halves are joined by a gutter that widens with the screen — the pair must meet on the centre line and spend the leftover on the outer edges. With no dimensions from the server nothing is wide.

nodes.label: GET /api/Reader/chapter-info pageDimensions
nodes.rationale: The vertical-scrolling view uses them to lay pages out, and so keep the slider in sync, before any image has loaded.

nodes.label: Serialized progress posts and the last-page rule
nodes.norm_label: serialized progress posts and the last-page rule
nodes.rationale: Posts go through a queue so a slow save cannot regress a later page, and the last page reports pages, not pages - 1, because Kavita only marks a chapter read when pagesRead >= pages. The initial page is saved on open, since onPageChanged never fires for it — deferred a frame, because it is reached from build and writing to a provider during build is what Riverpod refuses.

nodes.label: Two readings of null in the stored language
nodes.norm_label: two readings of null in the stored language
nodes.rationale: Never having chosen falls back to the device's default; choosing to follow the device is a person asking for the system's language, and the device default must not stand in for it. So the stored language is a code, the empty string for 'follow the device', and absent for no choice — the one place a sentinel earns its keep, since MaterialApp already spends null on the other meaning.

nodes.label: The vertical-scrolling view must be placed before it reports
nodes.norm_label: the vertical-scrolling view must be placed before it reports
nodes.rationale: A scroll view has no initialPage, so it opens at offset 0 while the reader is on page 40 and the first flick would report page 0 and post it back, wiping the place the chapter was opened at. It jumps after the first layout (offsets need the width) and _placed gags _onScroll until then.

nodes.label: accountIdFrom(token) — the key is derivable offline
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: accountidfrom(token) — the key is derivable offline
nodes.rationale: api/account_id.dart reads Kavita's nameid claim straight out of the JWT, so the user id half of the profile key is available on every path including a resume, and LoginResult needs no new field.

nodes.label: ProgressDto has no user field
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.rationale: POST /api/Reader/progress takes { volumeId, chapterId, pageNum, seriesId, libraryId, bookScrollId, lastModifiedUtc } with no user field; get-progress takes only chapterId and is documented as 'for the logged in user'; has-progress, continue-point, time-left and all eight mark-*read/unread endpoints are the same. Across the whole surface exactly one progress endpoint takes a user id — GET /api/Reader/first-progress-date?userId= — and it is a statistics read.

nodes.label: Server-side access gating (MemberDto.libraries, AgeRestrictionDto)
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.rationale: Library access is carried by the user (MemberDto.libraries, written through UpdateUserDto.libraries) and content is gated per account by AgeRestrictionDto { ageRating, includeUnknowns }. A persona that merely hid libraries would still hold a session that can fetch them: enforcement that lives in the client is not enforcement.

nodes.label: Local profiles / personas (rejected)
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.rationale: The obvious shape, used by every other family app on the device: one server account, several in-app personas with their own progress and filtered view. Rejected because Kavita cannot divide one account into two readers — two personas would share one progress row and fight over pagesRead — and because a client-side library filter would be a lie rather than a rule.

nodes.label: The lock belongs on unrestricted profiles
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: the lock belongs on unrestricted profiles
nodes.rationale: Because a child's age restriction protects their account rather than the device, the thing worth a PIN is the unrestricted session that opens everything — the opposite of where one would first think to put it. That asymmetry follows directly from Kavita enforcing restriction per account.

nodes.label: There is no kids mode to build
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: there is no kids mode to build
nodes.rationale: The protection a child gets is their own account's age restriction, enforced by the server. It protects the child's account, not the device, and does nothing at all if the child reads inside an adult's session.

nodes.label: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: a profile is exactly one kavita account
nodes.rationale: The app invents no personas. A device holds several profiles keyed by (normalized baseUrl, Kavita user id), and every request is made as exactly one of them. Both requirements — per-reader progress and per-reader library access — are met for free by signing in as the right account, and by nothing else.

nodes.label: An auth key is a whole account
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: an auth key is a whole account
nodes.rationale: It authenticates essentially the entire API, the handler builds a principal carrying every one of the user's role claims, and it is accepted from a query parameter, a header or a route value. So N profiles on one device is N complete, non-expiring account credentials in one keychain. Worse for a shared device: only the owning user can rotate one (authKey.AppUserId != UserId → BadRequest), and an admin 'invalidate' is cache eviction rather than invalidation — a parent cannot revoke a child's key, nor their own from a lost device.

nodes.label: The PIN is a speed bump between family members
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: the pin is a speed bump between family members
nodes.rationale: Because an auth key is a whole non-revocable account credential, the lock in front of a profile cannot be device security. The UI must say it keeps family members out of each other's profiles and must never imply it protects a lost device.

nodes.label: The catalogue dies with its profile
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: the catalogue dies with its profile
nodes.rationale: Removed in the same confirmation that already takes the lock, the preferences and the saved chapters — and not named in that copy, which lists what a person chose to keep and what it costs them. No expiry, because an old catalogue is strictly better than none. No cap and no Settings row, because it is hundreds of KB against an image cache measured in hundreds of MB and a clear button could only make the app worse offline. Clearing the image cache must not touch it.

nodes.label: The shared image cache's invariant is eroded
nodes.community_name: A profile is exactly one Kavita account
nodes.norm_label: the shared image cache's invariant is eroded
nodes.rationale: The shared key rests on 'the app only ever builds an image URL for content the server has already listed for the profile asking', which becomes '…at some point'. If access is revoked in Kavita then offline the catalogue still lists the library and builds its cover URLs, and the device's shared cache may hand back covers another profile fetched. Online it cannot outlive one fetch, because a successful fetch replaces the list. There is no offline fix — asking the server whether access still stands is precisely what an offline device cannot do — and what leaks is a cover picture of a series that profile had already been told about; every page is behind a request that will be refused.

nodes.label: ClientDevice headers (client_device.dart)
nodes.rationale: Three headers stamped by an interceptor rather than frozen into BaseOptions because one of them moves. X-Device-Id is a per-install UUID in secure storage, since Kavita's fallback fingerprint would collapse every Android install into one device. X-Kavita-Client must match the web UI's regex exactly or the sender is still stamped Web App and loses everything else.

nodes.label: ClientIdentity (app version read off the binary)
nodes.norm_label: clientidentity (app version read off the binary)
nodes.rationale: appVersion is read via package_info_plus rather than compiled in, so the version in the User-Agent is the version the tag built. Resolving never throws and falls back to 0.0.0 — deliberately not a copy of the current version, since a hardcoded one is the string that drifts. The build number is deliberately not shown or carried.

nodes.label: MangaFormat.isImageReadable (PDF reads, EPUB cannot)
nodes.rationale: PDFs read through the normal image reader because /api/Reader/image takes extractPdf, passed unconditionally (harmless elsewhere). EPUB is reflowable text with no image path at all — it needs the /api/Book endpoints and a reader of its own — so EPUB rows stay non-tappable and unsavable and the reader refuses them outright, since a deep link or a resume does not pass through the series screen.

nodes.label: offlineProvider
nodes.rationale: Flips true when a request fails to reach the server (dio connection/timeout) and back on the next success. It only moves when a request fails, so it cannot answer for a device that loses its connection while sitting on a screen — which is why the settings dot needed a probe.

nodes.label: PageLoading (page_loading.dart)
nodes.rationale: PDF extraction happens on the first request and can take a while, so the ordinary spinner shows and only after 1.8s and only for a PDF says what the server is doing — an ordinary page must never flash that text on its way in.

nodes.label: serverReachableProvider (GET /api/Health probe)
nodes.rationale: /api/Health is the right endpoint rather than a convenient GET: [AllowAnonymous] so it reports reachability even with a stale token, and [SkipDeviceTracking] so polling does not churn the ClientDevice entry. It runs through the client so it feeds offlineProvider in passing; being offline outranks a probe that once succeeded, and it re-runs on foreground resume because the four tabs live in an IndexedStack and nothing else would think to ask. A 500 or 404 counts as reachable. The state is said in words as well as colour, with the dot's Semantics merged into the card's node.

nodes.label: ios/Flutter/Release.xcconfig (Runner-target signing scope)
nodes.rationale: Target scope is the whole point: the same settings on xcodebuild's command line reach every target and Swift Package Manager plugin packages fail the archive with 'does not support provisioning profiles'. A target xcconfig also outranks the template's project-level CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY and keeps the team ID in a secret.

nodes.label: Android job: android/key.properties switch
nodes.rationale: build.gradle.kts reads key.properties if present and falls back to debug keys if not, so a fork and a fresh clone still build while Play gets a real signature. Output is an App Bundle because .aab is the only thing Play accepts.

nodes.label: Build number is github.run_number
nodes.rationale: Both stores want a monotonically increasing number; pubspec's +1 never moves and a version-as-number would repeat itself. run_number counts every run of this workflow file, so numbers jump between releases — increasing is the requirement, not consecutive. Renaming build.yml restarts the count at 1 and every later upload is rejected.

nodes.label: iOS job: signed TestFlight path or unsigned IPA fallback
nodes.norm_label: ios job: signed testflight path or unsigned ipa fallback
nodes.rationale: Chosen by whether this is a release ref AND the signing secrets exist, so a fork with no Apple credentials still builds green.

nodes.label: Play upload to the internal track
nodes.norm_label: play upload to the internal track
nodes.rationale: A third state gated on PLAY_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_JSON because the Play Developer API cannot create an application. 'tracks' must never be omitted (the action defaults to production); internal has no review delay and does not start the twelve-testers-for-fourteen-days clock that only a closed test does. The action is pinned to a commit, not a tag, because it is handed the service account key.

nodes.label: Releases are cut by a tag, not by a push
nodes.norm_label: releases are cut by a tag, not by a push
nodes.rationale: The tag IS the version: it is passed to --build-name, writing Android versionName and iOS CFBundleShortVersionString, so nothing in the repository has to be bumped and a shipped binary cannot disagree with the tag it was built from. Push one tag by name, never --tags, because GitHub creates no event for a push carrying more than three tags.
